item.title: Italian fashion brands Patrizia Pepe, Dixie under court supervision over labour exploitation in Bangladesh
item.description:
Italian fashion labels Patrizia Pepe and Dixie have been placed under court administration over the alleged exploitation of foreign workers in their supply chain in Tuscany, prosecutors and judicial sources said on Friday.

The measure targeted two companies that relied on unscrupulous subcontractors to lower production costs, Luca Tescaroli, chief prosecutor in the city of Prato, said in a statement, without naming them.

Judicial sources later confirmed the companies' identities.

A spokesperson for Patrizia Pepe had no immediate comment, while a spokesperson for Dixie did not immediately respond to a request from Reuters.

New wage structure for garment workers to take effect in December

Milan courts have taken similar moves in recent years against other well-known labels, including LVMH-owned LVMH.PA cashmere firm Loro Piana and units of fashion houses Valentino and Giorgio Armani, putting pressure on the entire Italian fashion industry to improve labour standards.

'Culpable inaction and no proper oversight'

Being placed under administration means that court-appointed external administrators will verify steps due to be taken by Patrizia Pepe and Dixie to meet judges' demands on the cleanup of their supply chains.

The two companies, however, are not under any criminal investigation.

The Florence court that placed them under supervision reprimanded them for "culpable inaction and failure to exercise proper oversight" on subcontractors who exploited Bangladeshi and Albanian workers, Tescaroli said.

The workers were poorly paid, forced to work long hours, denied holidays and constantly harassed and abused, Tescaroli said, adding that 18 of them who cooperated with investigators would be offered legal residence permits.

The prosecutor also said it was the first labour abuse case in the textile city of Prato involving Albanian subcontractors, saying they had adopted criminal practices traditionally associated with Chinese-owned sweatshops.

item.title: PM announces pay rise for Gram Police, govt to pay mobile bills
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Saturday announced a pay rise for Gram Police, lifting their monthly salary from Tk 7,500 to Tk 10,500 and their chiefs’ from Tk 8,000 to Tk 11,000.

The government will also pay monthly mobile phone allowance up to Tk 150 for each member.

The Prime Minister said the new arrangements will take effect from today. He said two additional women Gram Police members would be recruited in every union and their maternity leave would be extended to six months.

The Prime Minister made the announcements at a rally of Gram Police at the National Parade Ground in the capital, marking the historic National Revolution and Solidarity Day.

“At present, a Gram Police member’s monthly salary is Tk 7,500. We have raised it to Tk 10,500. The monthly salary of the Gram Police chief has been raised from Tk 8,000 to Tk 11,000,” the Prime Minister declared.

“The retirement gratuity has been raised from Tk 50,000 to Tk 80,000 for members and from Tk 80,000 to Tk 1 lakh for chiefs,” he announced.

The Prime Minister said a member of Gram Police will get Tk 150 monthly mobile phone allowance to facilitate them communication easier.

Gram Police members will get Tk 500 every week for travelling to police stations instead of Tk 300, he said adding the chiefs will get Taka 600 for this purpose.

Tarique Rahman said the government has taken initiative to raise the financial and professional dignity of Gram Police instead of only changing their designations.

“Those previously were known as ‘Mohalladar’ and ‘Dafadar’ will now be called as Gram Police member and Gram Police chief respectively,” he said.

The Prime Minister said two new women Gram Police members will be recruited in every union to empower women and increase employment. Maternity leave for women Gram Police will be for six months.”

In recognition of the work of Gram Police, he said, a long road in every union will be named after the force.

“Trees will be planted on both sides of the road, and the money from selling them will be distributed among the Gram Police members of that union,” he said.

The Prime Minister also said he would ask the Local Government Ministry to arrange new bicycles for members in every three to three and a half years, instead of every five.

PM’s wife Zubaida Rahman, also vice president of the Ziaur Rahman Foundation, was present on the occasion.

Gas supply rises as Summit LNG terminal resumes operations
item.description:
Gas supply to the national grid has returned to normal levels after Summit LNG’s floating terminal in Moheshkhali, Cox’s Bazar, resumed operations following maintenance.
The terminal restarted regasification at 1pm on Saturday, with Petrobangla confirming that both LNG terminals were once again supplying gas to the national grid at their usual levels.
According to Petrobangla’s data at 2pm on Saturday, the country’s total gas supply stood at 2,408 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd). Of this, 1,584mmcfd came from domestic gas fields, while LNG accounted for 824mmcfd.
The Summit terminal was shut down last Wednesday for maintenance, resulting in a significant drop in gas supply to the national grid.
At 8am that day, total gas supply stood at 2,540mmcfd, including 1,566mmcfd from domestic fields and 974mmcfd from LNG.
After the terminal was shut down, the total supply fell to 2,079mmcfd by 10am. Domestic gas supply remained almost unchanged at 1,565mmcfd, while LNG supply dropped to 514mmcfd.
This represented a decline of 461mmcfd in total supply within two hours.
Petrobangla had earlier said maintenance at the Summit terminal would continue from 8am on November 4 until 4pm on November 7, during which regasification would remain suspended. It had warned that the disruption could cause low gas pressure across the country.

item.title: Govt forms 6-minister committee to address employees’ pay and allowance discrepancies
item.description:
The government has taken steps to address discrepancies that have arisen over the order of pay grades, promotions and higher grades in the new pay structure for government officials and employees.

It has formed a six-member cabinet committee to review the complaints and recommend measures, including the reorganisation of pay grades, the introduction of new risk allowances and changes to existing allowance rates.

The committee, chaired by Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, has been formally named the ‘Committee for reviewing issues relating to the fixation, expansion and revision of employees’ pay grades and allowances’.

The committee will make recommendations on raising or lowering the pay grades of certain posts, ensuring consistency among different grades and introducing new allowances. The Cabinet Division issued a gazette notification on the matter on 2 November.

Higher salaries for govt employees Sunday, many face complications in determining pay

The other members of the committee are Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman, Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon, Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain, and State Minister for Public Administration and Food Md Abdul Bari.

According to the notification, the committee will examine complaints received from employees and make the necessary recommendations for their resolution.

It will be assisted by Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Ghani, Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister ABM Abdus Sattar, Finance Secretary Md Khairuzzaman Majumder and Public Administration Secretary Md Kamruzzaman Chowdhury. Secretaries of the relevant ministries and divisions will also provide assistance.

The Finance Division will provide secretarial support to the newly formed committee. The committee may include additional members if necessary. However, no deadline has been set for submitting its recommendations, and no timeframe has been announced for their implementation.

Government officials and employees therefore believe they will have to wait longer for the discrepancies in the pay structure to be resolved.

The committee will make recommendations on raising or lowering the pay grades of certain posts, ensuring consistency among different grades and introducing new allowances.

Pay is lower in higher grades

Employees in various posts and professions in government service have expressed dissatisfaction with their pay grades. They allege that some employees receive different pay grades despite performing similar duties, that grades do not correspond to the status of their positions, and that financial benefits decrease after promotion.

These discrepancies have become more apparent during the implementation of the new pay structure.

Employees from various offices, including the Finance Division, Financial Institutions Division, Ministry of Liberation War Affairs, Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology, and Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism, have raised questions about these issues.

Citing inconsistencies in seniority, the order of pay grades, higher grades and the fixation of house rent allowances, they recently submitted applications to Finance Secretary Md Khairuzzaman Majumder.

The applications cite examples of these discrepancies. One inconsistency in the new pay structure concerns the fixation of salaries for employees in grades 11 and 12.

Minimum salary in government jobs is Tk 33,000, what's the maximum?

Under the new structure, the starting basic salary for grade 11 is Tk 25,000, while for grade 12 it is Tk 24,300. Although grade 11 has a higher starting salary, the situation is reversed after the previous pay adjustments are taken into account.

An official explained the calculations to Prothom Alo. He said that as of 30 June, an employee in grade 11 had a basic salary of Tk 23,660. Under the previous structure, his salary had increased by Tk 11,160.

Adding this increase to the starting salary under the new structure brings the total to Tk 36,160. However, as there is no corresponding step for this amount in the new structure, his basic salary is set at Tk 37,000, the next step up.

The official added that an employee in grade 12 had a basic salary of Tk 23,580 at the same time. Under the previous structure, his salary had increased by Tk 12,280.

Under the new structure, the calculation comes to Tk 36,580. However, his basic salary is set at Tk 37,700, the next step up. As a result, the grade 12 employee receives Tk 700 more in basic salary than the grade 11 employee.

One inconsistency in the new pay structure concerns the fixation of salaries for employees in grades 11 and 12.

Income may decrease despite promotion

Another complaint from employees is that some may see their total income decrease after promotion. According to an example they provided, an employee in grade 10 has a basic salary of Tk 49,700. After being promoted to grade 9, the basic salary increases to Tk 51,000.

However, the rate of house rent allowance falls from 50 per cent to 45 per cent in the new grade, reducing the amount they receive. Previously, an employee in grade 10 received Tk 24,850 as house rent allowance. After promotion, this falls to Tk 22,950.

As a result, the employee’s combined income from basic salary and house rent allowance would decrease by Tk 600 after promotion.

Employees have also expressed dissatisfaction over higher grades. They allege that awarding higher grades based on completing a specified period of service brings the salaries of some senior and junior employees closer together.

In some cases, a junior employee may even end up earning more than a senior colleague.

Govt employees to get 3 months’ salary arrears with October pay, calculation starts tomorrow

Scope to introduce new risk allowances

The terms of reference of the six-member cabinet committee cover not only resolving discrepancies in pay grades but also upgrading or downgrading the grades of various posts and ensuring consistency between grades.

The committee will also be able to recommend introducing new risk and other allowances, as well as increasing or reducing the rates of existing allowances.

In other words, the committee’s terms of reference provide an opportunity to consider introducing new allowances for government employees engaged in hazardous duties. It will also be able to recommend revising the rates of various existing allowances.

An official from the Finance Division, speaking on condition of anonymity said, “A similar committee was formed after the 2015 pay structure was introduced. However, that committee was unable to make any contributions to resolving the complications at the time.”

The gazette notification on the new pay structure was issued on 17 September. Government employees were given until 25 October, from 5 October, to have their salaries fixed under the new structure. Those who completed the process during that 20-day period received higher salaries on 1 November, including arrears calculated under the new structure from July.

The government’s Integrated Budget and Accounting System (iBAS++) was used for this purpose. However, alongside technical difficulties in fixing salaries, some provisions of the gazette also required clarification.

An official from the Finance Division, speaking on condition of anonymity said, “A similar committee was formed after the 2015 pay structure was introduced. However, that committee was unable to make any contributions to resolving the complications at the time.”

“I hope this six-member ministerial committee will play a genuinely effective role in addressing the discrepancies this time,” he added.

item.title: Bangladesh challenges ousted PM Hasina to seek extradition as she requests new passport
item.description:
Bangladesh challenged on Monday ousted leader Sheikh Hasina to seek extradition from India if she was serious about returning home, while reviewing an application to renew her passport.

Hasina, whose 15-year rule was ended by a mass uprising she tried to crush, has vowed to return in December to Bangladesh, where she was sentenced to death for crimes against humanity over the 2024 crackdown on protesters.

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told reporters on Monday that authorities were looking into Hasina’s request for a new passport, adding that she was a convicted offender who had taken refuge abroad.

“The legal basis of the application, whether it followed due process, and whether there is a right to apply for a passport — all those matters are being reviewed,” he said.

“We had already sent a letter to that country (India) seeking her extradition through due process,” he added.

Hasina’s British lawyers have requested to renew her documents after the “reported revocation” of her passport.

A letter by law firm Matrix Chambers, addressed to Bangladesh’s high commission in New Delhi and seen by AFP, requested her passport renewal — but made no mention of when or where she planned to travel.

Md Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of the court that sentenced Hasina to death in November 2025, dismissed the application as “nothing but a political stunt”.

Hasina has said several times she intends to return, telling AFP in an email that she was “fully aware” she faced being hanged.

She has told Reuters she plans to return to surrender before a court, and her aides said on Monday the date would be announced once various formalities were completed.

Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh’s junior foreign minister, said she should simply surrender herself to face justice.

“Let her tell India: ‘Yes, there is an extradition treaty. Please hand me over. I killed this many people, and I am ready to face the sentence. Please execute me there’,” he told reporters.

“She is a thief, a bandit and a terrorist who fled… How could she, having fled, want to come back?”

‘Trying to create panic’

Hasina fled to old ally India in 2024, and has not been seen in public since but has taken part in online news conferences by telephone.

She was convicted and sentenced in absentia.

Her continued presence in India has strained ties between Dhaka and New Delhi, which says the extradition request is under legal review.

The government of Tarique Rahman, whose party won elections in February in which Hasina’s Awami League was barred from contesting, has said it would ensure the former prime minister receives due legal process in all cases against her should she return.

“In view of the reported revocation of her existing Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card (NID) by the interim government and other authorities, I respectfully request that you take the necessary steps to issue a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card for our client,” Hasina’s lawyers at London-based Matrix Chambers wrote to Preeti Rahman, acting high commissioner at Bangladesh’s embassy in Delhi.

The letter asked for the applications to be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of her Bangladeshi nationality and in accordance with “obligations arising under international human rights instruments”.

But Hasina’s pledge to return presents a political challenge for Rahman’s government.

Many Bangladeshis want to see her hanged, while others fear her return could galvanise her former supporters and trigger a fresh confrontation between rival camps.

Police on Monday said they had arrested 12 people for a series of petrol bomb attacks, including against property, an empty bus and police vehicles this month, without causing any casualties.

Dhaka police spokesman Md Akhtar Hossain said the suspects were members of Hasina’s banned Awami League party.

“They are trying to create panic among people,” he told AFP. “We are remaining vigilant to deal with any untoward situation.”

item.title: Bangladesh's external debt increases almost threefold in decade
item.description:
Bangladesh’s foreign debt has almost tripled in 10 years, a steeper rise than in any other South Asian country except the Maldives, according to the World Bank.

Even so, the country has a lower debt burden relative to export earnings than Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bhutan. However, its burden is higher than that of India and Nepal.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Report 2026, Bangladesh’s total foreign debt stood at $113 billion at the end of 2025, up from about $38 billion in 2015. That is the third-largest stock in South Asia.For every $100 in annual earnings, Bangladesh carries $210 in total debt and pays back $16 annually.

Economists say the indicators are manageable for now, but Bangladesh could face repayment trouble if borrowing keeps growing at this pace and the money is not put to proper use.

In the South Asia region, India holds the largest external debt stock at $764 billion, up 59pc in a decade. Pakistan follows at $135 billion, almost double the level of 10 years ago.

In Sri Lanka, foreign loans rose 31pc to $57 billion. External debt rose 186.5pc to $11 billion in Nepal and 57pc to $3.3 billion in Bhutan. The Maldives recorded a more than fourfold increase to $4.7 billion.

Repayments take 16pc of exports

Debt servicing took 16pc of Bangladesh’s export earnings in 2025, 3.1 percentage points less than the year before. That is the share of export income spent on repaying principal and interest on foreign loans, and a falling ratio is a positive sign of repayment capacity.

Even so, it remains above India and the South Asian average of 10pc, though below Sri Lanka at 26pc and Bhutan at 19pc. Measured against gross national income (GNI), servicing costs are low. At 2pc, Bangladesh matches India and the regional benchmark, against 5pc in Sri Lanka and 6pc in Bhutan.

The country’s debt-to-GNI ratio, which is external debt as a percentage of the national income, stands at 24pc. It is a manageable level but slightly above the South Asian aggregate of 21pc. The ratio is 20pc in India, 41pc in Pakistan and 54pc in Sri Lanka. Set against what the country earns from exports, the debt looks heavier.

External debt stands at 210pc of Bangladesh’s annual exports, more than twice what the country earns each year from foreign trade and other income.

That is far above India at 83pc and the South Asian aggregate of 95pc, but below Pakistan at 324pc, Bhutan at 301pc and Sri Lanka at 272pc.

Warning on borrowing

Zahid Hussain, a former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office, said Bangladesh still does better than Pakistan and Sri Lanka on these indicators but trails India. “If foreign debt keeps growing at the current pace, it would not be surprising if Bangladesh eventually faced a situation similar to Sri Lanka’s,” said the economist.

“If you are not prudent about the types of debt you take and how you use the borrowed funds, becoming another Sri Lanka is only a matter of time.” He said comparing Bangladesh with Pakistan is difficult, given Pakistan’s particular geopolitical and strategic situation.

Zahid said exports matter because the debt-to-GDP ratio shows very little about a country’s ability to repay. A large economy is not enough; it also needs adequate liquidity, which is why the export ratio is important.

On this measure, Bangladesh is also vulnerable because its export base is small and heavily dependent on a single product category. Its exports as a share of GDP are among the lowest, he said.

“Remittances add to foreign currency earnings, but even counting them India stays far ahead because its remittance income is much higher. Sri Lanka, similarly, receives large numbers of tourists and earns substantial foreign currency from tourism,” he added.

Costlier loans ahead

Prof Mustafizur Rahman, a distinguished fellow at local think tank Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said the debt-to-GDP and debt-to-export ratios are rising gradually, but the most important indicator is the ratio of net exports to debt servicing.

He said that about 85pc of export earnings come from readymade garments, where domestic value addition is 60-65pc. The ratios would therefore be significantly higher if net exports were used.

Recent loans carry relatively high interest rates and shorter repayment and grace periods, so the ratios will rise rapidly in the coming years, said Mustafizur, as Bangladesh already faces growing debt pressure. Government debt servicing was $4.9 billion in the last fiscal year and is projected to reach $7.6 billion by 2029, as interest rates climb while grace and repayment periods shrink. The interest rate in Japan, for example, has risen from below 1pc in 2021 to above 3pc, he said.

He said Bangladesh needs to raise exports and domestic value addition, improve domestic resource mobilisation and reduce its reliance on foreign borrowing to finance the Annual Development Programme.

“Global financing conditions are tightening. Bangladesh will still need foreign loans, but should negotiate better terms and secure more concessional financing,” he said, adding, “It could also consider raising funds through bond issuance.”

According to the World Bank report, foreign debt of developing countries rose 5.5pc to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, the fastest growth since 2021 and about four times the average pace of 2022-24.

Debt-service pressure remained severe amid elevated global interest rates. Low and middle-income countries paid $1.4 trillion in principal and interest in 2025, up 1.9pc and the fifth consecutive annual rise.

Between 2022 and 2025, developing countries paid $436 billion more in debt service than they received in new financing.—The Daily Star/

item.title: 21 killed as migrant boat sinks off Senegal
item.description:
DAKAR: A small boat carrying migrants sank off northwestern Senegal killing at least 21 people in the latest tragedy along the dangerous Atlantic Ocean route from Africa to Europe, authorities said.

The Senegalese interior ministry said that only one person had been rescued in addition to the 21 bodies recovered, which added to the thousands who have died in recent years trying to reach Spain’s Canary Islands from West Africa.

The ministry said the death toll was “provisional” and that the search was still going on. Media reports said the pirogue-type flat-bottom boat capsized on Saturday off the Loumpoul dunes in Kebemer department, between Dak­ar and the northern city of Saint-Louis.

However Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegal’s main migrant aid association Boza Fii, said that “the sinking occurred on Friday”. The nationalities of all the victims had not been confirmed, he said.

Greek coastguards rescue 28 from migrant boat off Crete

“But the bodies recovered yesterday (Saturday) are Senegalese,” he added. Thousands of people from We­­st Africa try each year to reach Eur­­ope on the perilous Atlantic route.

Senegalese authorities also said they had intercepted 142 migrants on Friday who were on a similar small boat aiming to reach Spain.

The group included 23 women, two babies and two other children, and were from Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria, according to police. The Senegalese government on Saturday stressed “its determination to combat people smuggling networks, notably through strengthened cooperation with neighbouring countries,” the interior ministry said in a statement.

Spanish authorities on the Canary Island of El Hierro declared an emergency on Saturday after a surge in migrant boat arrivals.

Boat in distress

Greek coastguards said on Sunday rescuers had found the body of a man and dragged to safety 28 other people on a migrant boat in distress off the island of Crete.

Maritime police launched an eme­rgency rescue after the boat issued an alarm signal, with winds of 40-50 kilometres an hour making sea conditions difficult, the coastguard said.

The survivors, all reportedly Sudanese, were picked up by another boat sailing nearby, then transferred to a police vessel and taken to the port of Heraklion on Crete, the agency said. On Wednesday, 59 people were reported missing after their boat capsized off the island, according to a 23-year-old Bangladeshi man who survived. No bodies have yet been found.

item.title: Anyone saying ‘December is at the door’ has no connection with Bangladesh: Adviser Titumir
item.description:
Those who are talking about the Awami League’s return next December have no connection with Bangladesh, said Professor Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, the Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning.

He said there was currently no one capable of reviving the Awami League, unlike the situation after 1975, when efforts were made to revive the party.

Professor Titumir described the “ousting of the Awami League” by the people of Bangladesh in 2024 as a victory for the country.

He made the remarks as the chief guest at a discussion titled “The Famine of 1974: Post-Independence Economic Crisis”, held at the Monsoon Theatre Hall of the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum on Sunday afternoon.

The discussion was the fifth instalment of the museum’s Democratic Journey Seminar Series.

“If anyone says that ‘December is knocking at the door’, it should be understood that they have no connection with the soil, grass or water of Bangladesh,” Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir said.

Titumir, a professor in the Department of Development Studies at Dhaka University, said the 1974 famine could not be explained solely by food shortages or failures in the market system. Rather, it was also rooted in the state’s estrangement from the people, a crisis of political legitimacy and the role of violence.

The prime minister’s adviser pointed to continuities between the systems of governance from 1972 to 1975 and the Awami League government’s rule from 2009 to 2024.

He said both periods were characterised by governments becoming detached from people’s aspirations and attempting to retain power through patronage and violence.

Titumir said similar tendencies were evident during both 1971–75 and 2009–24, including the suppression of opposition, abuse of state power and the use of violence to remain in office.

Rashe Al Mahmud Titumir said three theories are generally put forward to explain the 1974 famine. These concern a decline in overall food availability, people’s lack of purchasing power or access to food, and the absence of a social contract to prevent famine. The influence of international food aid and Cold War geopolitics is also cited.

However, he argued that these explanations fail to adequately address the crisis in the relationship between the state and its people.

According to the incumbent PM’s adviser, people’s aspirations were not reflected in the way the country was governed after independence. A disconnect developed between the people and those in power. In these circumstances, a system of patronage emerged as a means of retaining power, extending from rural areas to the centre. The influence of this patronage system was also evident in “rationing” and food distribution.

Titumir said similar tendencies were evident during both 1971–75 and 2009–24, including the suppression of opposition, abuse of state power and the use of violence to remain in office.

He also pointed to similarities in food prices during the two periods. While international rice prices fell, prices in the Bangladeshi market rose, he said. The international price of rice stood at US$147 per tonne in 1972 before rising to $542 in 1974. He noted that domestic prices in Bangladesh were higher than those in the international market during the same period.

The prime minister’s adviser further said that when the state becomes alienated from the people and resorts to violence to retain power, conditions conducive to famine and plunder emerge. Therefore, any discussion of the 1974 famine must consider not only economic statistics but also state violence and loss of life during that period.

Describing the 2024 mass uprising as a victory for the people, Titumir said Bangladeshis had repeatedly asserted their sovereignty. He said the people had played a role in establishing their rights in 1971, 1975, 1990 and 2024.

However, he stressed that making this victory sustainable required effective state institutions. Highlighting the role of the Jatiya Sangsad (national parliament), he said the state must retain the exclusive authority to exercise legitimate “violence”, but that authority must remain accountable.

An effective parliament was essential for this purpose, he said. Article 7 of the Constitution recognises the sovereignty of the people, and parliament is the institution through which this principle must be upheld. The challenges of state-building cannot be addressed through street movements without making parliament effective, he added.

Therefore, any discussion of the 1974 famine must consider not only economic statistics but also state violence and loss of life during that period.

The seminar was chaired by Ehsan Mahmud, director-general of the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum. Writer and treasurer of the Panam Institute Asif Iqbal, and economist and researcher Nahian bin Khaled, also spoke at the event.

item.title: Bangladesh takes climate justice demand to COP31
item.description:
Bangladesh will press for increased grant-based climate finance, stronger global commitments on adaptation and greater accountability from major polluters at the upcoming COP31 climate summit, seeking international support to tackle worsening climate impacts without adding to the country’s debt burden.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to attend the two-day World Leaders’ Summit on November 11–12, where he is expected to present Bangladesh’s priorities on climate justice, international financial commitments and support for implementing national climate plans.
The 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. It is expected to bring together world leaders, climate negotiators, development partners, civil society representatives and international organizations.
Bangladesh’s central message is that the countries bearing the greatest climate risks, despite contributing relatively little to global emissions, should not have to take on more debt to protect their people.
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo outlined the country’s negotiating priorities at a press conference at the Secretariat in Dhaka on Thursday.
Special Assistant to the Prime Minister for Environment and Climate Change Dr Saimum Parvez, Acting Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change Dr Fahmida Khanam, Additional Secretary Navid Saifullah and Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Managing Director Kazi Rawnaqul Islam were also present.
Mintoo said Bangladesh would prioritize climate justice, protection of vulnerable communities and international financial and technological support for implementing its climate commitments. He emphasized the need for adequate, predictable and accessible climate finance, primarily in the form of grants, alongside stronger support for adaptation and addressing loss and damage.
Separately, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said on Monday that Bangladesh would urge developed countries to provide climate finance as grants rather than loans and take responsibility for their contribution to global carbon emissions. Her remarks reinforce Dhaka’s position that climate finance should reflect the historical responsibility of major emitters and the financial needs of vulnerable developing countries.
Bangladesh has prepared a national position paper through consultations with relevant ministries, government agencies and climate experts. It will also coordinate its negotiating position with the Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group, the Group of 77 and China, and other climate-vulnerable countries.
Climate finance is expected to be one of Bangladesh’s principal priorities at COP31, with Dhaka seeking stronger implementation of commitments made by developed countries under international climate agreements. The country will call for new, additional, predictable and accessible resources to support adaptation, resilience-building and the implementation of national climate plans.
A key demand will be that assistance for climate-vulnerable developing countries should come primarily through grants instead of loans. Bangladesh argues that loan-based climate assistance can increase public debt and place an additional financial burden on countries already dealing with the economic consequences of climate change.
The government will also press for simpler application and approval procedures for international climate funds. Lengthy processes and complex administrative requirements, Bangladesh maintains, can prevent resources from reaching communities when they are most urgently needed.
The issue has wider significance for developing countries as they seek to bridge the gap between the scale of climate action required and the financial support currently available.
Earlier, at COP29 in Baku, countries agreed that developed nations would take the lead in mobilizing at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, within a broader effort to scale up climate finance from all sources to $1.3 trillion a year by the same deadline. For Bangladesh and other vulnerable nations, the challenge is to ensure that such commitments translate into accessible funding, particularly for adaptation and loss and damage.
Bangladesh will seek greater accessibility and effectiveness of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, established to assist developing countries particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change. Dhaka will advocate faster disbursement, simplified funding procedures and stronger support for communities facing irreversible climate impacts.
The country will also raise the importance of addressing non-economic losses, including displacement, disruption of traditional livelihoods and damage to cultural heritage and community identity. These concerns are particularly pressing for coastal and riverine communities in Bangladesh, where erosion, salinity intrusion, cyclones and other extreme weather events threaten homes, livelihoods and habitable land.
The government’s position is that international support must respond to the actual needs of affected populations rather than remain confined to financial pledges that are difficult to access. Bangladesh will therefore seek arrangements that allow vulnerable countries to respond to climate-related disasters while also investing in long-term resilience.
Bangladesh will call on countries to accelerate science-based greenhouse gas emission reductions in line with the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.
Dhaka will urge developed countries to demonstrate leadership in cutting emissions and call on major emitting economies to strengthen their climate commitments in line with their responsibilities and respective capabilities. It will also emphasize that developing nations need finance, technology transfer and capacity-building support to implement their nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
For Bangladesh, stronger global mitigation is essential because adaptation alone cannot eliminate the growing risks associated with continued warming. The government will argue that the countries with the greatest historical responsibility and financial capacity must take the lead in reducing emissions while supporting vulnerable nations to pursue climate-resilient development.
Implementation of Bangladesh’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP) will be another major focus of the negotiations. The government will seek financial and technological assistance to strengthen resilience in coastal areas, wetlands, river islands and drought-prone regions.
Priority areas include water security, food production, public health, disaster preparedness and the protection of climate-sensitive livelihoods. Bangladesh will also highlight the importance of early warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure and locally led adaptation initiatives.
Coastal communities facing cyclones and salinity intrusion, farmers affected by irregular rainfall and drought, and riverine populations confronting erosion and displacement are among those requiring stronger support. Dhaka will press for adaptation finance that reaches local communities and supports solutions shaped by their needs, traditional knowledge and direct experience of climate impacts.
Bangladesh will seek international cooperation to support a just and equitable transition towards low-carbon development across the energy, agriculture, industrial and transport sectors.
The government will emphasize that the costs and benefits of the transition must be distributed fairly, with particular attention to workers, low-income communities, women and young people. Skills development, social protection, labor rights and decent employment opportunities will be important elements of the country’s just transition agenda.
Dhaka will also advocate affordable access to renewable energy technologies, energy-efficient systems, cleaner industrial production and sustainable transport. Its position is that developing economies need international finance and technology to pursue cleaner growth without undermining employment, economic competitiveness or social development.
Bangladesh will explore opportunities to mobilize additional finance and technological support through international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The mechanism allows countries to cooperate in meeting their climate commitments, including through internationally transferred emission reductions and other forms of cooperation.
Dhaka considers carbon markets a potential supplementary source of finance for implementing its NDCs and supporting low-carbon development. However, the government will maintain that carbon market cooperation cannot replace predictable public climate finance, particularly for adaptation and loss and damage.
Bangladesh will also seek stronger international cooperation on affordable climate technologies, technical expertise and institutional capacity-building. Such support will be important for renewable energy, climate-resilient agriculture, industrial decarbonization, water management and disaster preparedness.
The country will advocate greater international support for conserving forests, mangroves, wetlands and biodiversity as part of its wider climate response. Nature-based solutions can strengthen ecosystem resilience while supporting local livelihoods and sustainable resource management. They are particularly relevant to Bangladesh, where mangrove forests, wetlands and river systems provide protection against climate hazards and support millions of people.
Bangladesh will also emphasize inclusive climate governance and meaningful participation by women, children, young people, persons with disabilities and marginalized communities. The government will seek improved access to climate finance for women-led and locally led initiatives, arguing that climate policies must reflect the needs and experiences of vulnerable populations.
Bangladesh is also expected to raise concerns about climate-related international trade measures that could affect the exports, employment and competitiveness of developing economies.
Dhaka will seek cooperation to ensure that environmental trade policies do not place disproportionate burdens on countries with limited financial and technological capacity. The government will advocate assistance to help industries adopt cleaner technologies, improve energy efficiency and meet evolving international environmental standards.
Its position will be that the shift towards sustainable production should be supported through finance, technology transfer and capacity-building rather than measures that could undermine development opportunities. For Bangladesh, the challenge is to balance global climate objectives with economic growth, employment generation and poverty reduction.
Bangladesh will establish a 100-square-metre pavilion at the COP31 conference venue to showcase its climate vulnerabilities, adaptation experience and national priorities.
The pavilion will feature the country’s updated nationally determined contribution, known as NDC 3.0, alongside its National Adaptation Plan and initiatives addressing climate-induced loss and damage. Other areas of focus will include climate finance, renewable energy, carbon markets, nature-based solutions and technological innovations supporting climate resilience.
The pavilion is expected to provide a platform for policy discussions, knowledge exchange and engagement with international development partners, research institutions and potential investors. Bangladesh also intends to highlight locally developed adaptation solutions and community experiences, demonstrating how people directly affected by climate change are responding to its impacts.
The government hopes the pavilion will help create opportunities for partnerships, technical cooperation and investment aligned with national climate priorities.
Bangladesh’s negotiating position will be guided by equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, a foundation of international climate cooperation. The principle recognizes that all countries have a role in addressing climate change, but their responsibilities and capacity to act differ according to historical circumstances and national capabilities.
Dhaka will argue that developed countries must fulfil their international commitments while providing vulnerable developing nations with the resources needed to implement climate action. The position also reflects a broader demand for accountability from major polluters, particularly as countries facing severe climate impacts struggle to finance adaptation and recovery.
For Bangladesh, climate justice is not limited to securing financial pledges. It also means ensuring that international support is accessible, reaches affected communities and reflects the scale of the damage they face.
COP31 comes at a critical point for international climate cooperation, with countries under growing pressure to turn existing commitments into measurable action.
Türkiye will host the conference, while Australia will chair the negotiations under the agreed organizational arrangement. Discussions are expected to focus on implementing the Paris Agreement, strengthening adaptation, mobilizing climate finance and supporting a fair transition towards cleaner energy systems.
With Prime Minister Tarique Rahman preparing to present the country’s position at the World Leaders’ Summit on November 11–12, Dhaka will seek to put grant-based finance, climate justice and the protection of vulnerable communities at the center of the discussions.
The success of COP31, from Bangladesh’s perspective, will ultimately depend not simply on new declarations but on whether international commitments deliver practical support to countries and communities already living with the consequences of climate change.

Hasina seeks passport to return, govt insists on extradition
item.description:
Former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has formally sought a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card to facilitate her planned return from India in December, but the government on Monday made clear that it wants her brought back through the extradition treaty rather than allowing her to return as a traveller.
The development, first reported by Reuters, marks Hasina’s first known formal communication with Bangladeshi authorities since she left for India following the mass uprising in August 2024.
While State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir dismissed the application and insisted on extradition, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the government was examining its authenticity, legal basis and procedural validity.
The International Crimes Tribunal’s chief prosecutor, meanwhile, described the move as a political stunt and questioned whether Hasina genuinely intended to return.
According to Reuters, lawyers from London-based Matrix Chambers sent a letter on Monday to Preeti Rahman, acting high commissioner at the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi.
The lawyers requested a new passport and NID for Hasina, citing the reported cancellation of her existing documents by Bangladesh’s interim government and other authorities.
They urged the mission to process the applications expeditiously, referring to her Bangladeshi nationality and obligations under international human rights instruments.
Hasina has previously told Reuters that she intends to return to Bangladesh in December and surrender before a court.
The former prime minister was sentenced to death in absentia by the International Crimes Tribunal in November 2025 over crimes against humanity committed during the crackdown on the 2024 student-led uprising.
She has denied the charges.
Responding to the development at the foreign ministry, State Minister Humaiun Kobir described Hasina’s application as “utterly ridiculous.”
He said Bangladesh would not issue an ordinary passport to facilitate the return of a fugitive convicted of serious crimes.
The state minister stressed that Bangladesh and India already had an extradition treaty and that Hasina’s return should be handled under that agreement.
“If she genuinely wants to return to Bangladesh, she should ask the Indian government to hand her over under the extradition treaty,” he said.
Kobir also criticised the British law firm representing Hasina, questioning the legal and ethical grounds for pursuing the application.
He acknowledged that individuals could engage lawyers and submit representations to authorities, but said doing so did not automatically establish entitlement to a passport.
According to media, diplomatic sources also questioned whether the application had been properly authorised, saying the email did not include a signed authorisation from Hasina.
The Bangladesh mission in Delhi forwarded the communication to the foreign ministry.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed adopted a more procedural position, saying the government was still verifying the reported application.
Speaking to reporters at the Secretariat, he said he had learned about the request through media reports but had not independently confirmed its authenticity.
The foreign and law ministries were examining whether the application had been submitted in accordance with the rules and whether Hasina was legally entitled to apply for the documents, he said.
The review would consider the relevant provisions of passport, citizenship and national identity laws.
Salahuddin reiterated that Bangladesh had already approached India through diplomatic channels seeking Hasina’s return under the bilateral extradition treaty.
He said the government would take the necessary steps after examining the legal issues.
International Crimes Tribunal Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam dismissed the application as an attempt to generate political attention.
“Whatever Sheikh Hasina is doing now is a political stunt. She will not come back,” he told reporters at the tribunal.
He said a formal press conference would be held on Tuesday, November 10, to explain the prosecution’s position on Hasina’s reported willingness to surrender.
The prosecutor’s remarks came as the government continued its efforts to secure the former prime minister’s return to face the consequences of the tribunal’s verdict.

item.title: Tarique-Erdogan meeting in Antalya today as Dhaka-Ankara ties grow closer
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Antalya, Türkiye, today, Tuesday.

The two leaders are scheduled to meet at 6:30pm local time at the Maxx Royal Hotel in Antalya. Diplomatic sources in Dhaka confirmed the information to Prothom Alo.

According to diplomatic sources in Dhaka, since the BNP government took office, relations between Dhaka and Ankara have grown closer through reciprocal visits by the two countries' foreign ministers, a visit to Türkiye by the Bangladesh Army chief and high-level contacts. Today's meeting is a continuation of that process.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman left Dhaka for Antalya this morning to attend the United Nations climate change conference (COP31). During the official visit from 10 to 12 November, the prime minister will lead the Bangladesh delegation. He will deliver Bangladesh's statement at the plenary session of the conference on 12 November.

On the sidelines of the conference, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman may hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of several countries, including the Turkish president.

This will be Tarique Rahman's second meeting with President Erdogan since he took office as prime minister.

The two leaders first met at the Turkish House in New York on 22 September, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. At the meeting, Erdogan called for placing bilateral relations on a more institutional footing. He emphasised expanding cooperation in the defence industry and increasing bilateral trade.

In early June, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan visited Dhaka. On the final day of his visit, he paid a courtesy call on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. During the meeting, Fidan said his visit was the first step towards elevating relations between the two countries to a strategic level.

Following the meeting, the two countries announced the formation of a joint committee at the ministerial level on defence and foreign affairs. The two sides also agreed to hold annual meetings between their foreign ministers and regular meetings involving the foreign and defence ministers.

During his visit to Dhaka, Fidan held a joint press conference with Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman. Khalilur Rahman thanked Türkiye for supporting Bangladesh's bid for the presidency of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Contacts between the two countries in the defence sector have increased over the past few years.

In July, Bangladesh Army Chief General Waker-Uz-Zaman visited Türkiye. During the five-day official visit, meetings focused on the existing friendly relations between the two countries, bilateral defence cooperation, military training, defence technology, cooperation in the defence industry, capacity building and various issues of mutual interest.

Both sides expressed interest in further expanding professional ties, exchanging experiences and strengthening defence cooperation between their armed forces in the future. As part of the visit, the army chief also inspected the operations of several leading defence industry and military technology institutions in Türkiye.

The Rohingya issue also features in Bangladesh–Türkiye discussions. At the meeting in New York, Erdogan praised Bangladesh for sheltering more than one million Rohingya. He expressed his country's commitment to continuing humanitarian assistance in areas including shelter, education and infrastructure for the Rohingya.

High-level contacts between the two countries have increased since the BNP government took office in February. Türkiye was represented at the swearing-in ceremony on 17 February by Deputy Foreign Minister Beris Ekinci.

After taking office, Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman made his first bilateral visit to Turkey on 14 March. During his meeting with Hakan Fidan in Ankara, a memorandum of understanding was signed between the diplomatic training institutes of the two countries. Khalilur Rahman also attended the Antalya Diplomacy Forum from 17 to 19 April. Hakan Fidan made his first visit to Dhaka in June.

item.title: Economy and reforms: LDC graduation window extended, challenges remain
item.description:
USA-TRUMP-TARIFFS-BANGLADESH-FACTORY

On 29 October 2026, during the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly UNGA), a decision was adopted to grant Bangladesh an additional three years to prepare for its graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category. Consequently, Bangladesh will now potentially graduate from the LDC group on 24 November 2029 instead of 24 November 2026.

This decision accords Bangladesh vital extra time to prepare. It also creates an opportunity to retain international support measures and trade preferences accorded to LDCs for a longer period. However, additional time alone will not eliminate the structural vulnerabilities of the economy. For that, concrete actions and tough decisions are imperative. Bangladesh must leverage this opportunity to execute significant and effective economic reforms.

The UN Committee for Development Policy (CDP) reviews the progress of LDCs every three years based on three criteria: Per Capita Gross National Income (GNI), the Human Assets Index (HAI), and the Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI). A country is considered for graduation if it meets the requisite thresholds in two consecutive triennial reviews. Bangladesh met these criteria for the first time in 2018 and again in 2021, prompting the CDP to recommend its graduation from the LDC category.

In view of the severe damage inflicted on the economy and development trajectory by the Covid-19 pandemic, the UN exceptionally granted Bangladesh, Laos, and Nepal a five-year preparatory period. As per the UN General Assembly resolution of 24 November 2021, Bangladesh’s graduation date was initially fixed for 24 November 2026. Under the latest decision, Bangladesh and Nepal have been granted a further three-year extension.

This additional timeframe offers Bangladesh a strategic window to address readiness gaps and implement plans for mitigating post-graduation challenges. During the preparatory phase, certain international support measures and trade benefits available to LDCs may continue under existing rules. However, uniform privileges will not apply across all markets, nor will the duration of these benefits be identical. Therefore, Bangladesh must immediately initiate bilateral engagements with its major trading partners. In particular, it must seek clarity regarding post-graduation tariff rates, rules of origin, and market access conditions.

The burden of enhancing competitiveness cannot rest on exporters alone. If the costs of power, energy, transport, logistics, customs clearance, and financing remain prohibitive, businesses cannot reduce unit production costs unassisted. The government must elevate the quality of these public services, while facilitating access to easy financing, technical advice, skill development programmes, and streamlined product certification systems.

To remain competitive in international markets, relying solely on duty-free access will not suffice. Prolonged port clearance delays, high transport costs, uninterrupted energy shortages, complex customs procedures, low productivity, and a narrow export basket must be addressed urgently. Operational efficiency at ports and in transport networks must be enhanced. Production lead times and costs must be curtailed. International labour rights and environmental standards must be upheld. Concurrently, businesses should be incentivised to produce higher value-added goods. Exporters also require targeted support to comply with rules of origin and technical requirements in global markets.

In this context, trade agreements can play a pivotal role. Bangladesh has already entered into several trade negotiations, notably the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) with Japan and the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with South Korea, both of which represent positive steps forward. However, before signing further agreements, the market dynamics of prospective partner countries, high-potential sectors, and specific contractual terms must be rigorously evaluated.

These agreements should look beyond mere import-export tariffs to encompass trade in services, investment, customs clearance, product standards, rules of origin, digital trade, and technological cooperation. Yet, signing agreements does not automatically equate to success. The true benchmark of success will lie in the extent to which export volumes and investment inflows increase, new technologies are transferred, and domestic enterprises benefit.

Bangladesh’s export basket remains overwhelmingly dependent on ready-made garments (RMG). Diversifying away from this concentration to boost non-RMG exports is critical. Potential exists to expand exports in pharmaceuticals, leather goods, processed agricultural products, light engineering goods, and IT-enabled services. Achieving this requires manufacturing goods to international standards, building a skilled workforce, ensuring uninterrupted power and energy supplies, modernising transport logistics, and reducing the cost of doing business. Furthermore, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) require financial and technological assistance to enable their entry into new export markets.

The burden of enhancing competitiveness cannot rest on exporters alone. If the costs of power, energy, transport, logistics, customs clearance, and financing remain prohibitive, businesses cannot reduce unit production costs unassisted. The government must elevate the quality of these public services, while facilitating access to easy financing, technical advice, skill development programmes, and streamlined product certification systems. Such measures will enable commercial enterprises to adopt modern machinery, conserve energy, minimise waste, and boost productivity, thereby creating new product lines to penetrate wider markets.

Reforming the import tariff regime is equally crucial. A major share of the government’s revenue is derived from import-stage taxes. However, high tariffs and supplementary duties inflate the import costs of raw materials and machinery for export-oriented industries, This in turn drives up production costs and erodes competitiveness in international markets.

That is why, tariff structures must be gradually simplified and rationalised through a clear, medium-term roadmap. Unnecessary tariff slabs should be consolidated, aligning duty structures with production and export needs. However, an abrupt reduction in tariffs could undermine government revenue. To offset this, revenue collection from direct income tax and Value Added Tax (VAT) must be enhanced by broadening the tax base and improving the efficiency of tax administration. Reducing reliance on import taxes will safeguard public spending in critical sectors such as education, health, and emergency infrastructure.

The extension of Bangladesh’s LDC graduation timeline comes at a juncture when the domestic economy has been grappling with multi-year headwinds. Under current circumstances, restoring macroeconomic stability must remain the paramount priority. Controlling inflation, bolstering revenue generation, mitigating external sector pressures, and enforcing good governance in the banking sector are indispensable for stimulating investment and production. Resolving these challenges demands deep-seated structural reforms.

The government’s Smooth Transition Strategy (STS) for LDC graduation must also be rigorously implemented. Its primary objective should be to preserve Bangladesh's export competitiveness, employment levels, and development momentum as LDC-specific preferences are phased out. The extra three years must not be viewed merely as a deferral of the deadline; this period must be utilised effectively to rectify economic vulnerabilities, enhance productivity, and prepare Bangladesh for international competition.

* Fahmida Khatun is an economist and Distinguished Fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD)
